newsitem.title: INDIA: India ACC results deepen cement worries.
newsitem.headline: India ACC results deepen cement worries.

text.p: Worse than expected first-half results by India's largest cement firm, Associated Cement Companies (ACC), stunned analysts and confirmed their bearish view on India's cement industry, hit by oversupply and slack demand.
ACC said late on Tuesday its net profit for the first half of 1996/97 (April-March) fell to 550.5 million rupees ($15.4 million), down 56 percent against the year-ago period.
Most analysts said on Wednesday they had expected ACC to post a net first-half profit of 800 million to 900 million rupees.
ACC shares fell 146 rupees, or 14 percent, to 1,010 rupees in noon trade on the Bombay Stock Exchange after the news.

"Contrary to expectations, the sales volume of cement during the six months ended 30 September, 1996, was only 2.4 percent higher than the corresponding period (in 1995) to visible slowdown of economic activity," ACC said in a statement.
"The company could not recover from an unprecedented increase in the cost of inputs that were beyond the company's control. As a result, the margin in cement business suffered," it said.
Analysts have been bearish about the cement industry because of oversupply in major markets and slackening demand.
Analysts said ACC's sales during the first half grew by 2.4 percent in volume terms and 9.4 percent in value terms, compared with the first half of 1995/95.
Increased prices for power, coal and freight raised the cost of production by more than 200 rupees per tonne, or 10 rupees per 50 kg bag, of cement in the first half, analysts said.
"Prices have been down since September," said Pradeep Mahtani, analyst at Jardine Fleming Broking in Bombay.
Mahtani said the industry should do somewhat better during January to March, when cement demand peaks.

"With the government acknowledging the slowdown of the Indian economy and issues leading to this slowdown yet to be addressed effectively, no respite is foreseen in the second half," said Manish Gupta, analyst at securities firm Khandwala Finances.
He said a possible price rise in petroleum products, seen later this year, would lead to higher electricity and freight costs for cement firms and hurt margins.

"Although the Cement Manufacturers Association has initiated measures to restrict damage through supply management -- they recently imposed a 10 percent production cut for all cement units -- the demand for cement remains a major cause for concern," Gupta said.
Analysts expect some recovery in prices in the New Year as producers realign their markets and work out new strategies.
India produced 69.31 million tonnes of cement during the 1995/96 financial year, according to official figures.
The nation has an annual capacity of 94 million tonnes, but produces only about 70 million tonnes, against annual demand of nearly 63 million. ($1 = 35.70 rupees)
